topics.title: Anatomy, physiology and pathophysiology: definitions and scope
topics.intro: Anatomy studies structure, physiology studies function, and pathophysiology explains how disease changes normal function.
points: Gross anatomy examines structures visible to the eye.
Histology examines tissues microscopically.
A disease mechanism connects structural change with functional consequences.
steps: Locate a structure.
Describe what it normally does.
Explain how a specific disturbance changes its function.

topics.title: Levels of structural organisation and body systems
topics.intro: The body is organised from chemical components to cells, tissues, organs and integrated organ systems.
points: Cells are the smallest living functional units.
An organ contains more than one tissue type.
Systems cooperate rather than acting independently.
steps: Molecules form cellular components.
Similar and supporting cells form tissues and organs.
Organs cooperate within systems to sustain the organism.

topics.title: Basic life processes
topics.intro: Living organisms carry out metabolism, responsiveness, movement, growth, differentiation and reproduction.
points: Metabolism includes building and breaking down molecules.
Responsiveness allows adjustment to internal and external changes.
Differentiation gives cells specialised roles.
steps: Nutrients and oxygen support metabolism.
Energy powers synthesis, transport and movement.
Cells respond, grow and maintain or reproduce their components.

topics.title: Anatomical terminology, positions, planes and directions
topics.intro: Anatomical terminology describes position consistently, independent of how a person is actually standing or lying.
points: In anatomical position, palms face forward.
Superior means toward the head; inferior means toward the feet.
Sagittal divides left/right, frontal anterior/posterior, and transverse upper/lower.
steps: Begin from anatomical position.
Choose a reference structure.
Describe direction or the plane through the body.

topics.title: Homeostasis and feedback systems
topics.intro: Homeostasis maintains internal conditions within workable ranges through coordinated feedback.
points: A receptor detects change; a control centre integrates information.
An effector produces the response.
Negative feedback opposes change; positive feedback amplifies it until an endpoint.
steps: A controlled variable moves away from its usual range.
Sensors inform a control centre.
Effectors alter the variable and the response is monitored.

topics.title: Cell structure and organelle functions
topics.intro: A human cell contains specialised structures that cooperate to maintain its environment and perform cellular work.
points: The membrane controls exchange and receives signals.
The nucleus contains most DNA; mitochondria produce much of the ATP.
Ribosomes, rough ER and Golgi cooperate in protein production and delivery.
steps: DNA information is transcribed into RNA.
Ribosomes translate messenger RNA.
Many newly made proteins enter ER-to-Golgi transport pathways.

topics.title: Transport across the cell membrane
topics.intro: Membrane transport moves substances across a selectively permeable lipid bilayer.
points: Simple and facilitated diffusion follow gradients without direct ATP use.
Active transport moves substances against an electrochemical gradient using energy.
Osmosis is net water movement across a selectively permeable membrane.
steps: Identify the substance and its gradient.
Determine whether the bilayer, channel, carrier or vesicle provides the route.
Distinguish passive movement from energy-dependent transport.
topics.question: Which process directly uses ATP to move ions against gradients?

topics.title: Cell division
topics.intro: The cell cycle coordinates growth, DNA replication and division. Mitosis produces genetically similar daughter nuclei.
points: DNA replicates during S phase of interphase.
Mitosis separates duplicated chromosomes; cytokinesis divides the cytoplasm.
Meiosis reduces chromosome number during gamete formation.
steps: Replicate DNA and prepare the spindle.
Align chromosomes and separate sister chromatids.
Re-form nuclei and divide the cytoplasm.

topics.title: Cell junctions
topics.intro: Cell junctions seal spaces, anchor neighbouring cells or allow direct communication.
points: Tight junctions restrict movement between epithelial cells.
Desmosomes resist mechanical stress.
Gap junctions allow ions and small molecules to pass between cells.
steps: Adjacent cells establish contact.
Junctional proteins form seals, anchors or channels.
The tissue gains barrier strength or coordinated activity.

topics.title: Cell communication: contact-dependent signalling
topics.intro: Contact-dependent signalling requires a membrane-bound signal on one cell to engage a receptor on a neighbouring cell.
points: The signal does not need to circulate in blood.
Direct cell contact provides spatial precision.
Receptor activation changes the target cell's behaviour.
steps: Two cells make contact.
A surface ligand binds a neighbouring receptor.
Intracellular signalling alters target-cell activity.

topics.title: Cell communication: paracrine signalling
topics.intro: Paracrine signals act locally on nearby cells after release into extracellular fluid.
points: Signals diffuse over short distances.
Local removal limits their range.
Autocrine signalling acts on the releasing cell itself.
steps: A cell releases a mediator.
The mediator reaches nearby responsive cells.
Receptor binding produces a local effect.

topics.title: Cell communication: synaptic signalling
topics.intro: Chemical synaptic signalling transfers information from a neuron to a target across a narrow cleft.
points: An arriving action potential opens voltage-gated calcium channels.
Calcium triggers neurotransmitter release.
Receptors on the target produce an excitatory or inhibitory response.
steps: An action potential reaches the terminal.
Vesicles release neurotransmitter into the cleft.
Receptors respond and transmitter is then removed.

topics.title: Cell communication: endocrine signalling
topics.intro: Endocrine signalling uses hormones carried in the circulation to reach distant target cells.
points: Only cells with suitable receptors respond.
Hormones may bind surface or intracellular receptors.
Feedback regulates many endocrine pathways.
steps: An endocrine cell releases hormone.
Blood distributes the hormone.
Target-cell receptors initiate a response.
topics.question: What carries endocrine hormones to distant targets?

topics.title: Epithelial tissue: types, locations and functions
topics.intro: Epithelial tissue covers surfaces, lines cavities and forms glands.
points: Cells are closely packed with little extracellular matrix.
Epithelium is avascular and rests on a basement membrane.
Shape and number of layers relate to protection, absorption or secretion.
steps: Identify the free surface and basement membrane.
Count cell layers and examine cell shape.
Relate the arrangement to the tissue's function.
topics.question: Which tissue lines the intestine and forms its absorbing surface?

topics.title: Connective tissue: types, locations and functions
topics.intro: Connective tissue supports, binds, protects and transports, with cells embedded in an extracellular matrix.
points: Matrix contains ground substance and fibres.
Examples include loose connective tissue, cartilage, bone and blood.
Collagen provides tensile strength; elastic fibres permit recoil.
steps: Cells produce matrix components.
Fibres and ground substance organise around cells.
The matrix gives the tissue its mechanical or transport properties.
topics.question: Which tissue family includes blood, bone and cartilage?

topics.title: Muscular tissue: types, locations and functions
topics.intro: Muscle tissue converts chemical energy into force through interactions between contractile proteins.
points: Skeletal muscle is striated and usually voluntary.
Cardiac muscle is striated, branched and joined by intercalated discs.
Smooth muscle lacks visible striations and contracts involuntarily.
steps: A stimulus activates the muscle cell.
Calcium makes contractile interactions possible.
ATP-dependent cross-bridge cycling generates force.

topics.title: Nervous tissue: structure, locations and functions
topics.intro: Nervous tissue detects information, processes it and communicates with other cells.
points: Neurons carry electrical and chemical signals.
Glial cells support, protect and regulate neuronal environments.
Dendrites usually receive inputs; axons conduct signals away from the cell body.
steps: Inputs reach a neuron.
Electrical activity propagates along its axon.
Synapses transfer information to the next cell.
topics.question: Which cell is specialised to transmit nerve impulses?

topics.title: Causes of cellular injury
topics.intro: Cell injury occurs when a stress exceeds the cell's capacity to adapt.
points: Causes include hypoxia, physical agents, chemicals, infections and immune reactions.
Severity and duration influence reversibility.
Energy failure, calcium imbalance and oxidative stress can reinforce one another.
steps: A harmful stimulus disturbs normal function.
The cell adapts or develops reversible injury.
Persistent severe injury can become irreversible.
topics.question: Which factor strongly influences whether injury is reversible?
topics.answer: Severity and duration of the insult
options: Severity and duration of the insult

topics.title: Cell membrane damage
topics.intro: Membrane damage disrupts selective permeability and the compartmental organisation of cells.
points: Plasma-membrane injury can cause ion imbalance and leakage.
Mitochondrial membrane injury interferes with ATP production.
Lysosomal membrane disruption can release digestive enzymes.
steps: Lipids or proteins in a membrane are damaged.
Ion gradients and compartment boundaries fail.
Swelling and enzyme-mediated damage may progress.

topics.title: Mitochondrial damage
topics.intro: Mitochondrial injury reduces energy production and can participate in cell-death signalling.
points: Reduced oxidative phosphorylation lowers ATP availability.
ATP-dependent ion pumps may fail.
Release of pro-apoptotic proteins can initiate apoptosis.
steps: An insult damages mitochondrial function.
Energy supply falls and ionic homeostasis deteriorates.
Severe injury promotes cell death.

topics.title: Ribosomal damage and impaired protein synthesis
topics.intro: Ribosomal dysfunction and rough-ER injury interfere with protein synthesis and processing.
points: ATP depletion can cause ribosomes to detach from rough ER.
Misfolded proteins activate the unfolded-protein response.
Persistent ER stress may lead to apoptosis.
steps: Protein synthesis or folding is disturbed.
Stress responses attempt to restore ER function.
Unresolved stress contributes to cell dysfunction or death.

topics.title: Nuclear damage
topics.intro: Nuclear injury includes DNA damage and characteristic nuclear changes in dying cells.
points: DNA damage activates repair and checkpoint pathways.
Pyknosis means nuclear shrinkage; karyorrhexis means fragmentation.
Karyolysis describes fading of nuclear staining through DNA breakdown.
steps: A damaging agent alters DNA.
Repair mechanisms and checkpoints respond.
Irreparable injury can lead to nuclear breakdown and cell death.

topics.title: Atrophy
topics.intro: Atrophy is a decrease in cell size that can reduce the size of a tissue or organ.
points: Reduced workload, innervation, nutrition or stimulation may cause atrophy.
Protein synthesis decreases and breakdown may increase.
It differs from hypoplasia, which reflects incomplete development.
steps: Demand or support decreases.
Cells reduce their structural components.
The affected tissue becomes smaller.

topics.title: Hypertrophy
topics.intro: Hypertrophy is an increase in cell size in response to greater workload or stimulation.
points: It can be physiological or pathological.
Muscle cells may enlarge by increasing structural proteins.
It differs from hyperplasia, which increases cell number.
steps: Workload or a trophic signal rises.
Cells increase protein and organelle content.
The tissue enlarges through larger cells.

topics.title: Hyperplasia
topics.intro: Hyperplasia is an increase in the number of cells in a tissue capable of division.
points: It may be a normal hormonal or compensatory response.
Pathological hyperplasia can follow excessive stimulation.
Hyperplasia is regulated and is not synonymous with cancer.
steps: A growth stimulus activates responsive cells.
Cell division increases.
Cell number and tissue size rise.

topics.title: Metaplasia
topics.intro: Metaplasia is replacement of one mature cell type by another better suited to a persistent stress.
points: It generally reflects altered differentiation of stem or progenitor cells.
It can be reversible after removal of the stimulus.
Protection may come at the cost of specialised function.
steps: Chronic irritation alters local signals.
Progenitor cells differentiate along another pathway.
A different mature cell type occupies the tissue.

topics.title: Dysplasia
topics.intro: Dysplasia is disordered growth and maturation with cellular atypia, often described in epithelial tissue.
points: Cells may vary in size, shape and nuclear appearance.
Normal tissue organisation is disturbed.
Dysplasia is not automatically invasive cancer but may be a precursor.
steps: Persistent injury or molecular changes disturb maturation.
Atypical cells and disorganised architecture develop.
Progression or regression depends on the underlying process.

topics.title: Cell swelling
topics.intro: Cell swelling is a common feature of reversible injury when water accumulates inside cells.
points: ATP depletion impairs sodium-potassium pumping.
Intracellular sodium increases and water follows.
Early swelling can reverse if the insult is removed.
steps: ATP availability falls.
Ion-pump function deteriorates.
Sodium and water accumulate in the cell.

topics.title: Intracellular accumulations
topics.intro: Intracellular accumulation occurs when a substance is produced, delivered or removed out of balance.
points: Materials include lipids, proteins, glycogen and pigments.
The substance may be normal but excessive, or abnormal.
The effect ranges from incidental change to cell dysfunction.
steps: Delivery or synthesis exceeds processing capacity.
Material accumulates in the cytoplasm or organelles.
Persistent storage may impair cell function.

topics.title: Cell death
topics.intro: Cell death includes necrosis and apoptosis, which differ in membrane integrity and inflammatory response.
points: Necrosis usually involves swelling and loss of membrane integrity.
Apoptosis forms membrane-bound fragments cleared by phagocytes.
Apoptosis can be physiological or pathological.
steps: A lethal insult or regulated death signal occurs.
Cell contents are disrupted or packaged into fragments.
Neighbouring cells and phagocytes remove the remains.

topics.intro: Medical terminology combines word roots, prefixes and suffixes to describe locations and processes.
points: Aetiology means cause; pathogenesis means mechanism of development.
A sign is observed; a symptom is experienced by the patient.
Acute and chronic describe time course, not necessarily severity.

topics.title: Skin structure and functions
topics.intro: Skin provides a barrier, sensation, temperature regulation and a role in vitamin D synthesis.
points: The epidermis is keratinised stratified squamous epithelium.
The dermis contains vessels, nerves, glands and connective tissue.
The hypodermis lies beneath the skin and contains variable fat.
steps: Epidermal cells mature toward the surface.
Dermal vessels and sweat glands help regulate heat exchange.
Sensory receptors detect changes in the environment.

topics.intro: Psoriasis is an immune-mediated inflammatory disorder with accelerated epidermal turnover.
points: Keratinocytes accumulate in thickened plaques.

topics.title: Dermatitis
topics.intro: Dermatitis describes skin inflammation and includes conditions with different initiating mechanisms.
points: Barrier dysfunction can promote dryness and irritation.

topics.intro: Leprosy is a chronic infection primarily affecting skin and peripheral nerves, caused mainly by Mycobacterium leprae.
points: Immune responses influence the pattern of disease.
Peripheral nerve damage may reduce sensation.
Sensory loss can predispose to unnoticed injury.

topics.title: Wound healing
topics.intro: Wound healing restores tissue continuity through overlapping phases of haemostasis, inflammation, proliferation and remodelling.

Granulation tissue contains new vessels and fibroblasts.
Collagen is reorganised during remodelling; healed tissue may not regain original strength.

Bone supports, protects, stores minerals and contributes to blood-cell formation.
Bone is living tissue that continuously remodels.

Relate compact and spongy regions to mechanical demands.

topics.title: Rheumatoid arthritis
topics.intro: Rheumatoid arthritis is a systemic autoimmune disease that commonly causes persistent synovial inflammation.

Cartilage and adjacent bone may be eroded.

topics.title: Osteoporosis
topics.intro: Osteoporosis reduces bone strength through loss of bone mass and deterioration of internal architecture.
points: Remodelling becomes imbalanced, with insufficient replacement of resorbed bone.
Trabeculae may become thinner and less connected.
Fracture risk increases even when mineralisation of remaining bone is normal.
steps: Bone resorption exceeds adequate formation.
Cortical and trabecular structure weakens.
Fragility fractures become more likely.

topics.title: Electrocardiogram
topics.intro: An electrocardiogram records body-surface electrical potential differences generated by cardiac activation.
points: The P wave represents atrial depolarisation.
The QRS complex represents ventricular depolarisation.
The T wave represents ventricular repolarisation; the tracing does not directly measure contraction force.
steps: Atrial depolarisation produces the P wave.
Ventricular depolarisation produces QRS.
Ventricular repolarisation produces the T wave.

topics.title: Hypertension
topics.intro: Hypertension is sustained elevation of systemic arterial pressure arising from interacting regulatory mechanisms.
points: Primary hypertension is multifactorial.
Increased vascular resistance and altered renal sodium handling can contribute.
Persistent pressure load can damage the heart, vessels, kidneys and other organs.
steps: Pressure-regulating systems become chronically imbalanced.
Arterial pressure remains elevated.
Vascular remodelling and target-organ stress develop.

topics.title: Cardiac arrhythmias
topics.intro: Arrhythmias are disturbances of the heart's rate or rhythm caused by abnormal impulse formation or conduction.
points: Mechanisms include altered automaticity, triggered activity and re-entry.
Rhythms may be fast, slow or irregular.
Effects on pumping depend on the rhythm and clinical context.

topics.title: Congestive heart failure
topics.intro: Heart failure occurs when cardiac function cannot adequately meet circulatory needs or requires abnormally raised filling pressures.
points: It may involve impaired contraction, impaired relaxation or both.
Neurohormonal responses can initially compensate but later worsen remodelling.
Congestion reflects elevated upstream pressures and fluid retention.
steps: Cardiac dysfunction reduces effective pumping or filling.
Compensatory neural and hormonal systems activate.

topics.title: Atherosclerosis
topics.intro: Atherosclerosis involves lipid accumulation and chronic inflammation within arterial walls.
points: ApoB-containing lipoproteins accumulate in the intima.
Macrophage foam cells and smooth-muscle responses contribute to plaque formation.
Plaque rupture or erosion can promote thrombosis.

topics.title: Coronary artery disease and myocardial ischaemia
topics.intro: Coronary artery disease commonly reflects atherosclerosis that limits blood supply to the myocardium.
points: Ischaemia occurs when oxygen supply fails to meet demand.
Fixed narrowing may limit increased flow during exertion.
Acute plaque complications can cause sudden obstruction.

topics.title: Angina
topics.intro: Angina is discomfort associated with transient myocardial ischaemia, without implying that infarction has occurred.
points: Stable angina is commonly provoked by increased demand with fixed coronary disease.
Unstable patterns can reflect acute plaque-related changes.
Coronary spasm is another mechanism of ischaemia.

An oxygen supply-demand mismatch develops.

topics.title: Myocardial infarction
topics.intro: Myocardial infarction involves death of myocardial tissue due to prolonged ischaemia.
points: An acute coronary thrombus after plaque disruption is a common mechanism.
Loss of viable muscle can impair contraction and electrical stability.
The extent of injury depends on severity, duration and collateral perfusion.
steps: Coronary oxygen delivery falls severely.
Sustained ischaemia causes irreversible myocyte injury.
